title: U.S.-Backed Consortium Signs Deal for Lukoil's International Oil Empire | OilPrice.com
text:
U.S.-Backed Consortium Signs Deal for Lukoil's International Oil Empire

US billionaire Todd Boehly has signed a deal with Lukoil to buy the sanctioned Russian oil company's international assets through a share swap backed by the US International Development Finance Corp (DFC), Reuters reported on Wednesday. The consortium will exchange Lukoil securities worth $10 billion for the assets.

The securities were bought from US and British funds and from US depositary banks that held them for retail investors, according to a person familiar with the terms.

Western investors' Lukoil shares were frozen after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and written down. "We're basically exchanging shares that are worthless to Americans ... for cash that is going back to them," said Boehly, chief executive of the asset manager Eldridge. The shares will be held in escrow in the UAE rather than going to Lukoil, the person said, to win approval from the Treasury Department, which has barred any windfall to the Russian company.

Two people familiar with the terms valued the portfolio at about $16 billion. It covers operations in 11 countries producing around 350,000 barrels per day, including oilfields in Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan, refineries in the Netherlands, Bulgaria and Romania, and a network of service stations that includes some in the United States. In early November, Reuters reported that the assets were initially valued at $22 billion.

Through the DFC, the US government will receive a share of future profits once the private investors recoup their capital and an agreed return, and it will have a role on the company's board. "Moving strategic energy infrastructure assets into US or allied partners' hands is a key policy priority of the administration," a DFC official said.

The deal needs approval from the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), and Boehly said closing could take up to a year.

The consortium now includes US bank Xtellus Partners and UAE-based Catena Investment Holding. Two partners left last week: the Syrian-Qatari Al-Khayyat brothers and Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company.

Washington sanctioned Lukoil in October 2025, which forced the company to sell its foreign holdings. Two earlier buyers failed to close. Gunvor withdrew its offer after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the trader the "Kremlin's puppet." Lukoil then agreed in January to sell the assets to Carlyle, excluding its stakes in Kazakhstan's Karachaganak and Tengizchevroil projects and the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, but OFAC never licensed that deal. OFAC has now issued 12 versions of its license for the sale talks. The latest, issued November 19, allows negotiations to continue until December 19.
